title: Song of Songs

stories.title: 💐 Song of Songs 1
summaryBullets: This is Solomon’s Song of Songs. (1:1).
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is more delightful than wine. (1:2).
The fragrance of your perfume is pleasing; your name is like perfume poured out. No wonder the maidens adore you. (1:3).
Take me away with you— let us hurry! May the king bring me to his chambers. We will rejoice and delight in you; we will praise your love more than wine. It is only right that they adore you. (1:4).
I am dark, yet lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon. (1:5).
Do not stare because I am dark, for the sun has gazed upon me. My mother’s sons were angry with me; they made me a keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have neglected. (1:6).
Tell me, O one I love, where do you pasture your sheep? Where do you rest them at midday? Why should I be like a veiled woman beside the flocks of your companions? (1:7).
If you do not know, O fairest of women, follow the tracks of the flock, and graze your young goats near the tents of the shepherds. (1:8).
I compare you, my darling, to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots. (1:9).
Your cheeks are beautiful with ornaments, your neck with strings of jewels. (1:10).
We will make you ornaments of gold, studded with beads of silver. (1:11).
While the king was at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance. (1:12).
My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh resting between my breasts. (1:13).
My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi. (1:14).
How beautiful you are, my darling! Oh, how very beautiful! Your eyes are like doves. (1:15).
How handsome you are, my beloved! Oh, how delightful! The soft grass is our bed. (1:16).
The beams of our house are cedars; our rafters are fragrant firs. (1:17).
crossRefs: Genesis 25:13: Kedar is named as a son of Ishmael, ancestor of the desert tribe whose black goat-hair tents are pictured here.
1 Samuel 24:1-3: David hides from Saul in the caves by the Rocks of the Wild Goats at En-gedi.
1 Kings 10:26-29: Solomon's chariot horses are imported from Egypt, a chariot costing six hundred shekels of silver.
Psalm 45:8: All your garments are fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia, from palaces of ivory.
1 Kings 5:6-9: Hiram's Sidonian loggers cut cedar and cypress in Lebanon and raft the timber down the coast to Solomon.

translationNotes.note: Hebrew has no separate word for best or greatest, so it doubles a noun instead: holy of holies for the innermost room, king of kings, vanity of vanities. Shir ha-shirim at 1:1 is that construction, and it means the finest song there is.

Two different Hebrew words sit behind the English. Ahavah is love in general, the word of Deuteronomy 6:5. Dodim, which 1:2 and 1:4 use, is narrower: the physical love between a husband and wife, and it is what Proverbs 7:18 puts in the mouth of the adulteress. English blurs the two into one word.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁחוֹרָה אֲנִי וְנָאוָה (shechorah ani ve-navah)
translationNotes.note: 1:6 says what the darkness is: the sun has looked on her because her brothers put her to work guarding the vineyards. Field labour marked a woman as poor, since a household with means kept its daughters out of the sun. She is answering a slight about her rank, not her ancestry, and the line ends with the complaint that she never got to keep her own vineyard.

Kedar was a nomad tribe of the north Arabian desert, descended from Ishmael's second son (Genesis 25:13), and famous enough that Isaiah 21:16-17 and Jeremiah 49:28-29 both name its flocks and tents. Those tents were woven from black goat hair, which sheds rain and bleaches nowhere. That is the black 1:5 is comparing her to, set against the fine curtains of Solomon in the same breath.

Kopher is henna, the Lawsonia shrub, whose cream-coloured flower clusters are heavily scented and whose dried leaves are ground into a paste that stains skin, nails and hair orange-red. The cluster at 1:14 comes from En-gedi, a freshwater spring in the cliffs on the western shore of the Dead Sea, a green pocket in bare desert and the place David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 24:1-2). A henna cluster from there is a luxury out of a wasteland.

A thick perfume oil pressed from the root of the Nardostachys plant, which grows in the Himalayas, so every drop in Israel had crossed the length of Asia. At 1:12 it is what she is wearing at the table. The flask Mary breaks over Jesus at Mark 14:3 was valued at three hundred denarii, and a denarius was a labourer's day wage (Matthew 20:2), so it was close to a year's pay.

Myrrh is the dried gum that bleeds from a cut in the Commiphora tree of Arabia and East Africa. It was one of the four spices in the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23), a burial spice (John 19:39), and mixed with wine a painkiller, which is what was offered at the cross (Mark 15:23). 1:13 describes a small cloth pouch of it worn on a cord between the breasts, so the scent lasted all night.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶרֶז (erez, cedar) - בְּרוֹת (beroth, cypress or juniper)
translationNotes.note: 1:17 makes beams and rafters out of the two most expensive timbers in the region. Cedar of Lebanon grows straight and tall and resists rot and insects, which is why Solomon imported it for the temple and the palace and paid Hiram of Tyre in wheat and oil for it (1 Kings 5:6-11). The couple are calling the open country their house and roofing it in royal wood.

stories.keyTakeaway: A woman expresses her longing for her beloved, describing his appeal and her own dark complexion; the two exchange admiration and affection, imagining intimate moments together.

headings.text: The Bride Confesses Her Love The Bride

stories.title: 💐 Song of Songs 2
summaryBullets: I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valley. (2:1).
Like a lily among the thorns is my darling among the maidens. (2:2).
Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest is my beloved among the young men. I delight to sit in his shade, and his fruit is sweet to my taste. (2:3).
He has brought me to the house of wine, and his banner over me is love. (2:4).
Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love. (2:5).
His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me. (2:6).
O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right. (2:7).
Listen! My beloved approaches. Look! Here he comes, leaping across the mountains, bounding over the hills. (2:8).
My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Look, he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, peering through the lattice. (2:9).
My beloved calls to me, “Arise, my darling. Come away with me, my beautiful one. (2:10).
For now the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. (2:11).
The flowers have appeared in the countryside; the season of singing has come, and the cooing of turtledoves is heard in our land. (2:12).
The fig tree ripens its figs; the blossoming vines spread their fragrance. Arise, come away, my darling; come away with me, my beautiful one.” (2:13).
O my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the crevices of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet, and your countenance is lovely. (2:14).
Catch for us the foxes— the little foxes that ruin the vineyards— for our vineyards are in bloom. (2:15).
My beloved is mine and I am his; he pastures his flock among the lilies. (2:16).
Before the day breaks and shadows flee, turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of Bether. (2:17).
crossRefs: Isaiah 35:1-2: The desert will blossom, and the splendor of Carmel and Sharon will be given to it.
1 Chronicles 27:29: A royal officer is set over the herds grazing in Sharon, the coastal plain named in this chapter.
Numbers 2:2: Each man camps under his own standard, with the banners of his father's house.
Leviticus 12:8: A mother who cannot afford a lamb brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons instead.
Judges 15:4-5: Samson turns three hundred foxes loose with torches and burns the standing grain, the vineyards and the olive groves.

translationNotes.term: Crocus of Sharon and lily of the valleys
translationNotes.note: Chavatstseleth appears only twice in Scripture, here and at Isaiah 35:1, and it is a bulb flower of open ground, rendered rose, crocus or meadow saffron. Shoshannah is a lily. Sharon is the coastal plain running north from Joppa, flat, well watered and thick with wildflowers in spring. 2:1 names common field flowers, not hothouse ones, and 2:2 is the reply that turns one of them into the only one.

Pressed cakes of dried grapes, dense and keeping well, handed out at feasts: David gave one to every person in Israel when the ark came up (2 Samuel 6:19). They were festival food, which is why 2:5 asks for them. Hosea 3:1 uses the same cakes for what Israel loved when it turned to other gods.

The banqueting hall, the room where wine was served and guests reclined. Over it at 2:4 is his degel, the standard a military unit marched under and pitched camp around (Numbers 2:2). The picture is a banner raised over her in public view, the opposite of a hidden affair.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּצְבָאוֹת אוֹ בְּאַיְלוֹת הַשָּׂדֶה (bi-tsva'oth o be-ayloth ha-sadeh)
translationNotes.note: An oath normally names God as witness. The one at 2:7 names wild animals, and the Hebrew for gazelles, tseva'oth, is spelled exactly like the word hosts in the title LORD of hosts. The refrain returns at 3:5 and 8:4. What it forbids is stirring love up before its time, and it is addressed to the daughters of Jerusalem, not to the lovers.

Israel has two seasons, not four. Rain falls from about October to April and then stops completely until autumn, so 2:11 is not a poetic mood but a date on the calendar. The turtledove of 2:12 fixes it further: that bird migrates in and its call is the sound of spring arriving, which is the point Jeremiah 8:7 makes about it.

The word covers both fox and jackal. They dig under the low stone walls of a vineyard, gnaw the roots and strip ripe fruit, which is why a vineyard was walled and given a watchtower and a lodge for a guard (Isaiah 5:1-2). 2:15 catches them at blossom time, when the damage costs the whole year's crop.

Rock doves nest on ledges in cliff faces where nothing can climb to them, and the hill country of Judea is cut with those gorges. 2:14 is calling a bird out of a place no hand reaches. Jeremiah 48:28 uses the same picture for people fleeing to the crags to survive.

Bether comes from a root meaning to cut in two, and the same word is used for the halves of the animals cut for the covenant at Genesis 15:10. So 2:17 either names a place or calls them the cleft hills, and either way it ends the scene with him going and rough ground between them.

stories.keyTakeaway: The woman describes her beloved as outstanding among other men and recounts intimate moments of affection; he then calls her to come away with him, praising her beauty and inviting her into the spring season, and she affirms their mutual belonging.

headings.text: The Bride’s Admiration The Bride The Bridegroom

stories.title: 🦌 Song of Songs 3
summaryBullets: On my bed at night I sought the one I love; I sought him, but did not find him. (3:1).
I will arise now and go about the city, through the streets and squares. I will seek the one I love. So I sought him but did not find him. (3:2).
I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city: “Have you seen the one I love?” (3:3).
I had just passed them when I found the one I love. I held him and would not let go until I had brought him to my mother’s house, to the chamber of the one who conceived me. (3:4).
O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right. (3:5).
Who is this coming up from the wilderness like a column of smoke, scented with myrrh and frankincense from all the spices of the merchant? (3:6).
Behold, it is Solomon’s carriage, escorted by sixty of the mightiest men of Israel. (3:7).
All are skilled with the sword, experienced in warfare. Each has his sword at his side prepared for the terror of the night. (3:8).
King Solomon has made his carriage out of the timber of Lebanon. (3:9).
He has made its posts of silver, its base of gold, its seat of purple fabric. Its interior is inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem. (3:10).
Come out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze at King Solomon, wearing the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding— the day of his heart’s rejoicing. (3:11).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 8:7: The turtledove and seasonal awareness.
Judges 15:4: Foxes noted elsewhere (different context).
Song of Songs 8:14: Gazelle imagery and closing invitation.
Song of Songs 3:5: Refrain locations.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַשֹּׁמְרִים הַסֹּבְבִים בָּעִיר (ha-shomrim ha-sovevim ba-ir)
translationNotes.note: The words say the watchmen who go around in the city, so this is a patrol, not a man standing on a tower. City gates were shut at dark (Joshua 2:5) and the watch walked the walls and streets until morning; Psalm 127:1 and Isaiah 62:6 both name them. Meeting them at 3:3 means she is out in a city under curfew.

A group addressed throughout the book, at 1:5, 2:7, 3:5, 5:8, 5:16 and 8:4, who question her and are put under oath by her. They function the way a chorus does, giving the woman someone to speak to on stage. They are never named or described further.

translationNotes.term: Columns of smoke from the wilderness
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְקֻטֶּרֶת מוֹר וּלְבוֹנָה מִכֹּל אַבְקַת רוֹכֵל (mequtteret mor u-levonah mi-kol avqat rokhel)
translationNotes.note: Frankincense and myrrh are resins from southern Arabia, and they reached Israel by camel up the desert road, a trade so valuable it built the cities along it. 3:6 says all the scented powders of the merchant, so the procession arrives smelling of imported goods and trailing incense smoke like a dust column.

Gibborim is the word for David's own elite, and 2 Samuel 23 numbers those at thirty, so sixty is twice the royal guard. 3:8 says each has his sword on his thigh against terror in the night, which is what an escort was actually for; a wedding party moved after dark and the roads were not safe.

Appiryon occurs only here in the whole Old Testament. It is a carried chair or couch on poles, lifted by men, and 3:10 gives the build: posts of silver, a base of gold, a seat of purple. Nothing about it moves under its own power; it exists so the person inside never touches the road.

Argaman, the purple of the seat at 3:10, is the dye taken from the murex sea snail, harvested and crushed on the Phoenician coast at Tyre and Sidon, where mounds of the broken shells are still there. It took thousands of snails to yield a few grams, so purple cloth was priced beyond ordinary reach and became the colour of kings. Exodus 25:4 lists it among the materials for the tabernacle, and Acts 16:14 has Lydia trading in it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּעֲטָרָה שֶׁעִטְּרָה־לּוֹ אִמּוֹ (ba-atarah she-itterah lo immo)
translationNotes.note: The atarah at 3:11 is not the royal crown of state but a wreath worn by a bridegroom on his wedding day, and Isaiah 61:10 describes a bridegroom decking himself with one. His mother sets it on him, which is her part in the ceremony. The verse dates the scene to the day of his wedding and the gladness of his heart.

stories.keyTakeaway: The beloved invites in springtime; vineyard care is urged; a night search in the city ends with finding and bringing him home; the charge not to awaken love is repeated.

headings.text: Solomon Arrives on His Wedding Day

stories.title: 👑 Song of Songs 4
summaryBullets: How beautiful you are, my darling— how very beautiful! Your eyes are like doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down Mount Gilead. (4:1).
Your teeth are like a flock of newly shorn sheep coming up from the washing; each has its twin, and not one of them is lost. (4:2).
Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your mouth is lovely. Your brow behind your veil is like a slice of pomegranate. (4:3).
Your neck is like the tower of David, built with rows of stones; on it hang a thousand shields, all of them shields of warriors. (4:4).
Your breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle grazing among the lilies. (4:5).
Before the day breaks and the shadows flee, I will make my way to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense. (4:6).
You are altogether beautiful, my darling; in you there is no flaw. (4:7).

Come with me from Lebanon, my bride, come with me from Lebanon! Descend from the peak of Amana, from the summits of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of the lions, from the mountains of the leopards. (4:8).
You have captured my heart, my sister, my bride; you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your neck. (4:9).
How delightful is your love, my sister, my bride! Your love is much better than wine, and the fragrance of your perfume than all spices. (4:10).
Your lips, my bride, drip sweetness like the honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the aroma of Lebanon. (4:11).
My sister, my bride, you are a garden locked up, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed. (4:12).
Your branches are an orchard of pomegranates with the choicest of fruits, with henna and nard, (4:13).
with nard and saffron, with calamus and cinnamon, with every kind of frankincense tree, with myrrh and aloes, with all the finest spices. (4:14).
You are a garden spring, a well of fresh water flowing down from Lebanon. (4:15).
Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind. Breathe on my garden and spread the fragrance of its spices. Let my beloved come into his garden and taste its choicest fruits. (4:16).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 3:8-9: Mount Hermon is called Sirion by the Sidonians and Senir by the Amorites.
1 Kings 10:16-17: Solomon makes five hundred hammered gold shields and hangs them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
Exodus 30:22-25: The sacred anointing oil is blended from liquid myrrh, fragrant cinnamon, fragrant cane and cassia in olive oil.
Genesis 2:8-10: The LORD God plants a garden in Eden with a river flowing out of it to water the ground.
Isaiah 58:11: You will be like a well-watered garden, like a spring whose waters never fail.

translationNotes.note: Four heights on the northern frontier. Hermon is the highest ground in the region at about 9,230 feet, snow-capped most of the year; Deuteronomy 3:9 says the Amorites called that same mountain Senir. Amana is the ridge the Amana river runs from toward Damascus, the Abana of 2 Kings 5:12. 4:8 adds the lions' dens and the leopards' hills, and both animals lived in that country.

Gilead is the wooded highland east of the Jordan, grazing country for generations. The goats of the region are black and long-haired, and a herd coming down a slope reads as a single dark sheet moving. That is the picture behind the hair of 4:1, and 4:2 answers it with white: ewes just washed and shorn, paired and none missing.

translationNotes.term: The tower of David hung with shields
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶלֶף הַמָּגֵן (eleph ha-magen, a thousand shields)
translationNotes.note: Shields were hung on a wall as trophies and as display. Solomon made two hundred large shields and three hundred small ones of beaten gold and hung them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon (1 Kings 10:16-17), and Shishak of Egypt carried them off (2 Chronicles 12:9). Ezekiel 27:11 has Tyre's walls hung the same way. 4:4 is describing armour on stonework, not jewellery.

translationNotes.term: A garden locked, a spring sealed
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גַּן נָעוּל (gan na'ul) - גַּל נָעוּל מַעְיָן חָתוּם (gal na'ul ma'yan chathum)
translationNotes.note: Both halves of 4:12 are about ownership. A garden in that climate was walled and gated because water and fruit were worth stealing, and a spring or cistern was capped and sealed with clay stamped by its owner, the same way a document was sealed. The image is property that belongs to one man and is closed to everyone else.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּפֶר (kopher, henna) - נֵרְדְּ (nerd, nard) - כַּרְכֹּם (karkom, saffron) - קָנֶה (qaneh, cane) - קִנָּמוֹן (qinnamon, cinnamon) - אֲהָלוֹת (ahaloth, aloes)
translationNotes.note: None of these grew in Israel and every one of them arrived by caravan. Saffron is the three red stigmas inside a crocus flower, picked by hand, and it takes roughly seventy-five thousand blossoms to make a pound. Qaneh is the aromatic cane, and cinnamon is bark; both are ingredients of the holy anointing oil at Exodus 30:23. The list is the contents of a treasury, priced as such.

Not the aloe vera plant on a windowsill. The ahaloth of 4:14 is fragrant aloeswood, the resin-soaked heartwood of the Aquilaria tree from southeast Asia, burned or shaved for its scent and one of the most expensive woods traded anywhere. Psalm 45:8 has a king's robes smelling of it, Proverbs 7:17 has a bed perfumed with it, and John 19:39 has Nicodemus bring seventy-five pounds of aloes and myrrh for a burial.

Living water means running water from a spring, as against the still water standing in a cistern. The distinction was legal, not poetic: the law requires living water for cleansing a healed leper (Leviticus 14:5-6) and for mixing the ashes of the red heifer (Numbers 19:17). 4:15 puts a spring inside the sealed garden of 4:12, so the enclosure has its own source.

Sister here is a term of address between lovers, used six times in 4:9 through 5:2 and nowhere else in the book. Kallah is the bride, and it is also the word for a daughter-in-law, since a bride entered her husband's father's household. Naming her both at once claims her as family before the marriage and as wife in it.

translationNotes.term: The north wind and the south wind
translationNotes.note: In Israel the north wind is cold and dry off the mountains and the south wind is hot off the desert, and 4:16 calls for both. Wind is what carries scent off a garden to anyone downwind. The verse ends by handing the garden to its owner, which is the point the whole locked-garden image has been building to.

stories.keyTakeaway: The lover delivers an extended praise of his beloved, comparing her eyes, hair, teeth, lips, and body to beautiful natural features and objects; he invites her to come away with him and describes her love, beauty, and mystery using garden and spice imagery.

headings.text: Solomon Admires His Bride The Bridegroom

stories.title: 👑 Song of Songs 5
summaryBullets: I have come to my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spice. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, O friends, and drink; drink freely, O beloved. (5:1).

I sleep, but my heart is awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking: “Open to me, my sister, my darling, my dove, my flawless one. My head is drenched with dew, my hair with the dampness of the night.” (5:2).
I have taken off my robe — must I put it back on? I have washed my feet— must I soil them again? (5:3).
My beloved put his hand to the latch; my heart pounded for him. (5:4).
I rose up to open for my beloved. My hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with flowing myrrh on the handles of the bolt. (5:5).
I opened for my beloved, but he had turned and gone. My heart sank at his departure. I sought him but did not find him. I called, but he did not answer. (5:6).
I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city. They beat me and bruised me; they took away my cloak, those guardians of the walls. (5:7).
O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you, if you find my beloved, tell him I am sick with love. (5:8).
How is your beloved better than others, O most beautiful among women? How is your beloved better than another, that you charge us so? (5:9).
My beloved is dazzling and ruddy, outstanding among ten thousand. (5:10).
His head is purest gold; his hair is wavy and black as a raven. (5:11).
His eyes are like doves beside the streams of water, bathed in milk and mounted like jewels. (5:12).
His cheeks are like beds of spice, towers of perfume. His lips are like lilies, dripping with flowing myrrh. (5:13).
His arms are rods of gold set with beryl. His body is polished ivory bedecked with sapphires. (5:14).
His legs are pillars of marble set on bases of pure gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, as majestic as the cedars. (5:15).
His mouth is most sweet; he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem. (5:16).
crossRefs: Exodus 3:8: The LORD promises to bring Israel up to a good and spacious land flowing with milk and honey.
Psalm 127:1: Unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain.
Isaiah 62:6: Watchmen are posted on the walls of Jerusalem who will never be silent day or night.
1 Kings 10:18-20: Solomon's great throne of ivory overlaid with pure gold, with twelve lions on its six steps.
1 Kings 7:2-3: The House of the Forest of Lebanon, built on four rows of cedar pillars under cedar beams.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִכְלוּ רֵעִים שְׁתוּ וְשִׁכְרוּ דּוֹדִים (ikhlu re'im shethu ve-shikhru dodim)
translationNotes.note: 5:1 answers the invitation at the end of chapter 4: he has come into the garden, gathered and eaten. Then a third voice speaks, telling companions to eat and drink deep. It stands at the exact middle of the book, and it is the only line addressed to the guests rather than between the two.

translationNotes.term: The bolt and the hand at the opening
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִן־הַחֹר (min ha-chor, through the hole) - כַּפּוֹת הַמַּנְעוּל (kappoth ha-man'ul, the handles of the bolt)
translationNotes.note: A door was barred by a wooden bolt slid into a socket in the frame, with pegs dropping into holes to lock it. The key was a wooden bar with pins to match, pushed through a hole cut in the door and worked from outside; keys that size were carried on the shoulder, which is the picture at Isaiah 22:22. 5:4 has a hand through that hole and 5:5 has myrrh left on the bolt.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רְדִידִי (redidi, my wrap or shawl)
translationNotes.note: The same night patrol she met at 3:3 finds her again at 5:7, and this time they beat her, wound her and strip off her wrap. A woman abroad in the streets after the gates were shut had no standing to be there. The redid is an outer shawl, named again only at Isaiah 3:23 in the list of finery stripped from the daughters of Zion.

Cholah is genuinely ill, the word used of a body that is sick, not a figure for feeling low. It appears at 2:5 and again at 5:8, where she puts the daughters of Jerusalem under oath to carry a message if they find him. The book treats the effect of love on the body as a physical fact and says so twice.

Two stones in the description at 5:14. Tarshish is a golden-yellow stone set in the fourth row of the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:20), rendered beryl, topaz or chrysolite. Sappir is lapis lazuli, deep blue shot with gold flecks of pyrite, quarried in what is now northeastern Afghanistan and carried west across the whole ancient trade network. It is not the modern sapphire.

5:11 says his hair is wavy and black as a raven, against a head described as finest gold. Grey hair carried honour in Israel (Leviticus 19:32, Proverbs 16:31), so raven black is a statement about his age: he is a young man in full strength, not an elder.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶשֶׁת שֵׁן (esheth shen, a work of ivory) - שֵׁשׁ (shesh, alabaster or white marble)
translationNotes.note: 5:14-15 builds him out of luxury materials. Ivory came from elephant tusk traded up from Africa and India; Ahab built an ivory-panelled house (1 Kings 22:39) and Amos 3:15 and 6:4 name ivory beds as the mark of a class the prophets indicted. Shesh is the pale stone used for columns. The whole description is a statue in expensive stock, deliberately.

stories.keyTakeaway: The lover arrives at night seeking entry; the woman hesitates, and when she finally opens the door he has vanished. Distressed, she searches the city, is beaten by watchmen, and describes her beloved's physical beauty in detail to the daughters of Jerusalem.

headings.text: The Bride and Her Beloved The Bridegroom The Friends The Bride

stories.title: 🌙 Song of Songs 6
summaryBullets: Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Which way has he turned? We will seek him with you. (6:1).
My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to pasture his flock in the gardens and to gather lilies. (6:2).
I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me; he pastures his flock among the lilies. (6:3).
You are as beautiful, my darling, as Tirzah, as lovely as Jerusalem, as majestic as troops with banners. (6:4).
Turn your eyes away from me, for they have overcome me. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down from Gilead. (6:5).
Your teeth are like a flock of sheep coming up from the washing; each has its twin, and not one of them is lost. (6:6).
Your brow behind your veil is like a slice of pomegranate. (6:7).
There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number, (6:8).
but my dove, my perfect one, is unique, the favorite of the mother who bore her. The maidens see her and call her blessed; the queens and concubines sing her praises. (6:9).
Who is this who shines like the dawn, as fair as the moon, as bright as the sun, as majestic as the stars in procession? (6:10).
I went down to the walnut grove to see the blossoms of the valley, to see if the vines were budding or the pomegranates were in bloom. (6:11).
Before I realized it, my desire had set me among the royal chariots of my people. (6:12).
Come back, come back, O Shulammite! Come back, come back, that we may gaze upon you. Why do you look at the Shulammite, as on the dance of Mahanaim? (6:13).
crossRefs: Song of Songs 3:2-3: Earlier city search and encounter with watchmen.
Psalm 141:2: Prayer like incense; lips and lilies imagery (fragrance motif).
Proverbs 27:9: Oil and perfume rejoice the heart (scent imagery).
Song of Songs 2:16: Earlier “My beloved is mine, and I am his.”

translationNotes.note: 6:4 pairs her with two cities, and the pairing is deliberate: Tirzah was the capital of the northern kingdom and Jerusalem the capital of the southern one. Kings reigned from Tirzah from Jeroboam onward, Zimri burned the palace down over himself there (1 Kings 16:18), and Omri ruled six years in it before he bought the hill of Samaria and moved (1 Kings 16:23-24). It sat about seven miles northeast of Shechem. The name itself means pleasing.

translationNotes.term: Awesome as an army with banners
translationNotes.note: Ayom is what makes an enemy flinch; Habakkuk 1:7 uses it of the Chaldeans. Nidgaloth comes from degel, the standard each division of Israel camped and marched under (Numbers 2:2). So the compliment at 6:4 and again at 6:10 is that looking at her is like watching a formed army come over a ridge with its colours up.

A royal household in the ancient Near East was counted this way because most of those marriages were treaties: a king sealed an alliance by taking the other king's daughter. A concubine was a wife of lower legal rank whose sons did not inherit first. 1 Kings 11:3 counts Solomon's at seven hundred and three hundred. 6:8-9 sets the whole roster against one woman and says she is the only one.

Egoz is the walnut, named only here in the Old Testament, and a walnut grove needs steady water, so 6:11 puts the scene in a watered valley. The verse is a walk to check the season, whether the vines have budded and the pomegranates have bloomed, which is ordinary spring work in a vineyard and the same errand as 7:12.

The Hebrew of 6:12 is the hardest line in the book. The words are chariots, my people, and noble or willing, and they can be read as a proper name, Ammi-nadib, or as the chariots of my noble people. English versions divide, and the app leaves the line as the text has it rather than choosing for the reader.

The only name or title the woman is given in the whole book, and it appears twice, both in 6:13. It carries the definite article, the Shulammite, which is how a person is marked by their town, and its consonants are those of shalom, peace, and of Solomon's own name. Scripture gives no further identification.

Machanayim means two camps, and it is a real town in Gilead east of the Jordan. Jacob named it after the angels of God met him there (Genesis 32:2), it was a Levitical city (Joshua 21:38), and David sheltered in it when Absalom drove him out of Jerusalem (2 Samuel 17:24). So 6:13 asks why they stare at her as at the dance of two camps, and the name can be read as the place or as the picture.

stories.keyTakeaway: A nighttime visit is missed; the watchmen beat and strip her veil; she gives a detailed description of her beloved and affirms, “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine.”

headings.text: Together in the Garden The Friends The Bride

stories.title: 🏵️ Song of Songs 7
summaryBullets: How beautiful are your sandaled feet, O daughter of the prince! The curves of your thighs are like jewels, the handiwork of a master. (7:1).
Your navel is a rounded goblet; it never lacks blended wine. Your waist is a mound of wheat encircled by the lilies. (7:2).
Your breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle. (7:3).
Your neck is like a tower made of ivory; your eyes are like the pools of Heshbon by the gate of Bath-rabbim; your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, facing toward Damascus. (7:4).
Your head crowns you like Mount Carmel, the hair of your head like purple threads; the king is captured in your tresses. (7:5).
How fair and pleasant you are, O love, with your delights! (7:6).
Your stature is like a palm tree; your breasts are clusters of fruit. (7:7).
I said, “I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit.” May your breasts be like clusters of the vine, the fragrance of your breath like apples, (7:8).
and your mouth like the finest wine. May it flow smoothly to my beloved, gliding gently over lips and teeth. (7:9).
I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me. (7:10).
Come, my beloved, let us go to the countryside; let us spend the night among the wildflowers. (7:11).
Let us go early to the vineyards to see if the vine has budded, if the blossom has opened, if the pomegranates are in bloom — there I will give you my love. (7:12).
The mandrakes send forth a fragrance, and at our door is every delicacy, new as well as old, that I have treasured up for you, my beloved. (7:13).
crossRefs: Numbers 21:25-26: Heshbon was the royal city of Sihon king of the Amorites before Israel took it.
Ezekiel 16:10: I clothed you in embroidered cloth and gave you sandals of fine leather.
Jeremiah 46:18: One will come who is like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea.
Psalm 92:12: The righteous will flourish like a palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon.
Genesis 30:14-16: Reuben finds mandrakes in the field at wheat harvest and Rachel trades a night with Jacob for them.

translationNotes.note: Heshbon stood on the plateau east of the Jordan and was the royal city of Sihon king of the Amorites until Israel took it (Numbers 21:25-26); Moab held it later (Isaiah 15:4). A town on that dry tableland lived off cut reservoirs, which is what the pools of 7:4 are. Bath-rabbim appears nowhere else in Scripture, and the verse identifies it as a gate of Heshbon.

translationNotes.term: The tower of Lebanon facing Damascus
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּמִגְדַּל הַלְּבָנוֹן צוֹפֶה פְּנֵי דַמָּשֶׂק (ke-migdal ha-Levanon tsopheh pene Dammaseq)
translationNotes.note: 7:4 names a lookout on the northern frontier watching the road to Damascus, the Aramean capital and the standing threat from the north for most of Israel's history. A migdal was a stone watchtower set to see an army coming while there was still time to send word. The comparison is to something that stands straight and misses nothing.

Carmel is the wooded ridge that runs from the Mediterranean coast inland, rising to about 1,700 feet, and it is the headland a ship sees first coming up that shore. Elijah met the prophets of Baal on it (1 Kings 18:19-20). The word also means garden land, so 7:5 crowns her head with a mountain that is a byword for being green when everything else has burned off.

The date palm grows a bare trunk sixty feet or more with the fruit only at the crown, so the harvester climbs it with a rope and cuts the clusters down; a good tree carries well over a hundred pounds of dates in a season. 7:7-8 uses that literally, the stature and the climbing and the taking hold of the branches. Deborah judged under a palm (Judges 4:5) and Jericho was called the city of palms.

This noun occurs three times in the whole Old Testament and no more: Genesis 3:16, where it is the woman's toward her husband; Genesis 4:7, where sin's is toward Cain; and 7:10, where it is his toward her. English uses ordinary words like desire or longing for it, so a reader cannot see that the Song is picking up a word that has been used only twice before, both times in Genesis.

The mandrake is a low Mediterranean plant with a thick forked root and small yellow fruit that ripens around the wheat harvest and smells strongly. It had a long-standing reputation for helping a woman conceive, which is the whole point of Genesis 30:14-16, where Rachel trades a night with Jacob for the mandrakes Reuben found. 7:13 has them giving off their scent at the door.

translationNotes.term: New and old over the door
translationNotes.note: A household stored the year's fruit on shelves and in jars set by the entry, where the crop from last season sat beside this season's. 7:13 says every choice fruit, new and old, is laid up there for him. It is the language of a full storeroom, which is what security looked like in an agricultural year.

stories.keyTakeaway: The lover praises the beloved's body in elaborate detail, comparing her features to natural and architectural landmarks; the beloved affirms her devotion and invites him to the countryside where she will give him her love.

stories.title: 🏵️ Song of Songs 8
summaryBullets: O that you were to me like a brother who nursed at my mother’s breasts! If I found you outdoors, I would kiss you, and no one would despise me. (8:1).
I would lead you and bring you to the house of my mother who taught me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the nectar of my pomegranates. (8:2).
His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me. (8:3).
O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right. (8:4).
Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved? I roused you under the apple tree; there your mother conceived you; there she travailed and brought you forth. (8:5).
Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm. For love is as strong as death, its jealousy as unrelenting as Sheol. Its sparks are fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all. (8:6).
Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away. If a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly scorned. (8:7).
We have a little sister, and her breasts are not yet grown. What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for? (8:8).
If she is a wall, we will build a tower of silver upon her. If she is a door, we will enclose her with panels of cedar. (8:9).
I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers. So I have become in his eyes like one who brings peace. (8:10).
Solomon had a vineyard in Baal-hamon. He leased it to the tenants. For its fruit, each was to bring a thousand shekels of silver. (8:11).
But my own vineyard is mine to give; the thousand shekels are for you, O Solomon, and two hundred are for those who tend its fruit. (8:12).
You who dwell in the gardens, my companions are listening for your voice. Let me hear it! (8:13).
Come away, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices. (8:14).
crossRefs: Genesis 38:18: Judah hands over his seal, his cord and his staff as a pledge, the seal standing for the man himself.
Haggai 2:23: I will make you like My signet ring, for I have chosen you, says the LORD of Hosts.
Deuteronomy 6:8: Tie these words as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads.
Genesis 29:18-20: Jacob serves seven years for Rachel, and they seem like a few days to him because of his love.
Matthew 21:33-41: A landowner plants a vineyard, walls it, digs a winepress and leases it to tenants for a share of the fruit.

translationNotes.term: If only you were my brother
translationNotes.note: 8:1 is not a wish to be related to him. A woman could greet a brother with a kiss in the street and nobody would think anything of it; showing affection to a man who was not kin in public brought contempt. She is saying she wishes she could touch him outside without paying for it, and 8:2 then takes him indoors to her mother's house.

A seal was a man's legal identity, not an ornament. It was cut from stone as a cylinder worn on a cord at the throat, or set as a stamp in a ring worn on the hand, and pressing it into clay signed a document and marked property as his. Judah hands over his seal and cord as a pledge (Genesis 38:18), Jezebel seals letters with Ahab's seal so they carry the king's authority (1 Kings 21:8), and Haggai 2:23 has the LORD make Zerubbabel like His signet ring. The heart and the arm named in 8:6 are the two places a seal was actually worn.

Sheol is the Old Testament word for the grave and the realm of the dead, where all descend (Genesis 37:35, Psalm 16:10), and the Septuagint renders it with the Greek hades. What 8:6 draws on is one property of it: Sheol does not let go and never gives anything back. Qin'ah is rendered jealousy or ardour and is the same word used for God's own zeal at Exodus 20:5.

One Hebrew word at the end of 8:6, built from shalhevet, a flame, with the ending yah, the short form of the divine name that also closes hallelujah. It is the only place in the Song where any form of the name of God appears at all. Versions render it a most vehement flame or the very flame of the LORD, depending on whether the ending is read as a superlative or as the name.

translationNotes.term: All the wealth of his house
translationNotes.note: Marriage in Israel was contracted with a mohar, a bride price weighed out by the groom's family to the bride's (Genesis 34:12, Exodus 22:16-17). 8:7 puts that transaction on the table and says a man offering the entire estate of his house for love would be utterly despised, which is the one thing in the book priced and then refused a price.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּיּוֹם שֶׁיְּדֻבַּר־בָּהּ (ba-yom she-yedubbar bah, the day she is spoken for)
translationNotes.note: 8:8-9 is the brothers holding a family council. A girl's marriage was negotiated by the men of her household, and their question is what they will do when the offer comes. A wall gets battlements of silver and a door gets barred with cedar planks; either way they are deciding in advance what they will build around her. 8:10 is her answer, that she is a wall already.

A place named nowhere else in Scripture; the name reads as owner of a multitude. 8:11 has Solomon leasing the vineyard out to tenants, which is how a large holding was worked: the tenant farms it and pays the owner a fixed sum out of the crop. 8:12 then sets the arrangement aside, my own vineyard is before me.

Rent on a leased vineyard, paid in weighed silver rather than coin. A shekel ran about four tenths of an ounce, so a thousand shekels is roughly twenty-five pounds of metal. Isaiah 7:23 prices planted vines at a thousand silver shekels for a thousand vines, one shekel a vine, which puts a vineyard of that rent at about that size. The two hundred held back at 8:12 for the men who tend the fruit is a fifth of the total.

stories.keyTakeaway: The woman wishes her lover were her brother so she could show him affection publicly, declares that love is stronger than death and cannot be extinguished by any force, and urges him to come to her swiftly. She also reflects on protecting her younger sister and claims her vineyard as her own possession.

intro:
Song of Songs was written by Solomon, son of David and third king of Israel, who is identified in the opening line as the author ("The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's," 1:1). Jewish tradition holds that Solomon composed this work in his youth, around 970-965 BC, near the start of his forty-year reign. The same Solomon who later wrote Proverbs in his middle years and Ecclesiastes in his old age; tradition orders the three Solomonic books according to the stage of life in which each was composed. 1 Kings 4:32 records that Solomon "spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005"; Song of Songs is "the song of songs" (a Hebrew superlative meaning "the greatest song"), the chief of those 1,005. Solomon was the son of David and Bathsheba, born in Jerusalem and raised under Nathan the prophet's tutelage; God appeared to him at Gibeon at the start of his reign and granted him unmatched wisdom along with riches and honor (1 Kings 3:5-14). The historical setting is the early decades of the United Monarchy, with Israel at its territorial and economic peak, trading with Tyre under Hiram I (Phoenicia), Sheba (modern Yemen), and Egypt's 21st Dynasty; Solomon had recently married the daughter of a Pharaoh of Egypt (1 Kings 3:1, his first political marriage); his neighboring kingdoms (Edom, Moab, Ammon, the Aramaean states) remained tributaries; and the Neo-Assyrian Empire was rising in the north but had not yet pressed into the Levant.

Song of Songs is the twenty-second book of the Christian Old Testament. In the Hebrew Bible it is one of the Five Megillot (Five Scrolls) within the Ketuvim (Writings), traditionally read aloud in synagogues at the Feast of Pesach (Passover, the spring festival commemorating the Exodus). The Hebrew name Shir HaShirim is a superlative construction meaning "the song of songs," that is, "the greatest of songs"; the English titles "Song of Songs," "Song of Solomon," and "Canticles" (from the Latin Vulgate Canticum Canticorum) all translate that phrase. The Greek Septuagint name Asma Asmaton (3rd century BC) is the same construction. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Song of Songs were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the 1st century BC.
